## New York Medical Bill Bankruptcy and Credit Reporting [2026]
Source: https://medicalbillbankruptcy.com/states/new-york.html

← medicalbillbankruptcy.com home

New York Medical Bill Bankruptcy and Credit Reporting [2026]

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New York residents.

New York Medical Bill and Credit Reporting Protection

New York has enacted a state-law ban on medical debt appearing on consumer credit reports. Fair Medical Debt Reporting Act (S4907A, 2023) bans medical debt on CR This stacks on top of the federal CFPB 2025 rule (which removes most medical debt from credit reports nationwide) and the Fair Credit Reporting Act - giving New York consumers one of the strongest protections against medical-debt credit destruction in the country.

RuleNew York Standard

State medical-debt CR banSTATE BAN

Primary citationN.Y. Gen. Bus. Law 380-v

Hospital financial-assistance (FAP)N.Y. Pub. Health Law 2807-k (Indigent Care Pool) + IRC 501(r)(4)

Price-transparency mandateNew York Hospital Financial Assistance Reporting

Pre-litigation rules5-day pre-suit notice + hospital financial assistance offer (GBL 519)

This page is about medical bills - the pre-discharge hospital invoices that have not yet been sold, charged off, or litigated. For post-collection medical debt that has already cycled through lawsuits and credit reporting, see the companion site medicaldebtbankruptcy.com.

Hospital Financial-Assistance Policy (FAP) Requirement in New York

N.Y. Pub. Health Law 2807-k (Indigent Care Pool) + IRC 501(r)(4)

IRC 501(r)(4) is the federal baseline for non-profit hospitals: to maintain tax-exempt status, the hospital must adopt a written Financial Assistance Policy, widely publicize it, and offer discounted or free care to eligible patients. The 2014 IRS final rule also requires:

501(r)(5) limitation on charges: FAP-eligible patients cannot be charged more than the "amount generally billed" (AGB) to insured patients.

501(r)(6) billing and collection: No extraordinary collection actions until the hospital has made reasonable efforts to determine FAP eligibility.

If your New York hospital skipped FAP screening before sending your bill to collections, you have a Section 501(r)(6) claim that can void the collection effort.

Section 501(r)(6) - Extraordinary Collection Action Bar

The 501(r)(6) rule is one of the most under-used patient protections. It requires tax-exempt hospitals to:

Wait at least 120 days from first billing before any extraordinary collection action (ECA).

Provide a plain-language summary of the FAP with each bill during the 120-day window.

Accept FAP applications for at least 240 days from first billing.

Extraordinary collection actions include:

Credit reporting the debt

Filing a lawsuit

Placing a lien on property

Garnishing wages

Seizing bank accounts

If your New York hospital took any ECA without FAP screening, file a complaint with the IRS and demand retraction of the collection action.

CFPB 2025 Federal Medical-Debt Rule

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 2025 rule removes most medical debt from consumer credit reports nationwide, including in New York. The rule specifically:

Prohibits creditors from using medical information in most credit decisions.

Removes medical-debt collection tradelines under $500 after 1 year.

Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing medical-debt information for non-medical credit decisions.

The rule is separate from state-law bans and works in parallel. Where New York has its own state-law ban, the stricter rule controls.

Pre-Litigation Notice in New York

5-day pre-suit notice + hospital financial assistance offer (GBL 519)

Many states now require hospitals to send a pre-suit notice offering a payment plan, FAP application, or charity-care screening before filing a collection lawsuit. In New York, the key pre-suit protections are captured in the rule above.

If the New York hospital skipped the notice or payment-plan offer, you may have:

A state-law claim to dismiss the lawsuit

An FDCPA claim against the collector (for attempting to collect on a defective claim)

A state unfair-trade-practices claim against the hospital

Medical Bill vs Medical Debt - Why the Distinction Matters in New York

This site focuses on medical bills: pre-discharge invoices from hospitals, providers, and specialists before they are sold to debt buyers. Bills have:

A direct provider relationship (you can negotiate, apply for FAP, set up payment plans)

Stronger legal protections (501(r), state HFA laws, pre-suit notice)

Higher negotiation leverage (providers will often accept 30-50% of billed)

Medical debt (covered at medicaldebtbankruptcy.com) is what the bill becomes after it is sold, charged off, or litigated:

Held by debt buyers, not providers

Subject to FDCPA and debt-validation rules

Often bought for 2-5 cents on the dollar, so settlements possible at steep discount

Strategy on the bill stage (this site) focuses on preventing the debt. Strategy on the debt stage focuses on resolving it.

New York Federal Bankruptcy Data

When hospital medical bills exceed income-based payment plans, bankruptcy discharges the debt and protects future wages and accounts. These FJC numbers show how New York debtors use the bankruptcy remedy for unpayable medical bills.

Bankruptcy as a Medical-Bill Discharge Tool in New York

When medical bills exceed your ability to pay through FAP, payment plans, and negotiation, bankruptcy discharges them. Medical debt is typically a general unsecured claim with no special treatment - it discharges in Chapter 7 within 90 days and is paid pro rata (often at cents on the dollar) through a Chapter 13 plan.

Key bankruptcy tools for New York medical debtors:

Chapter 7 discharge within 90-120 days

11 U.S.C. 362 automatic stay halts collection, garnishment, and lawsuit within 24 hours

11 U.S.C. 522(f) judicial lien avoidance against medical judgments impairing exemptions

Chapter 13 hardship discharge if medical condition prevents plan completion

Check 1328(f) refiling screener and the New York means test.

501(r)(5) limitation on charges: FAP-eligible patients cannot be charged more than the "amount generally billed" (AGB) to insured patients.

501(r)(6) billing and collection: No extraordinary collection actions until the hospital has made reasonable efforts to determine FAP eligibility.

If your Oklahoma hospital skipped FAP screening before sending your bill to collections, you have a Section 501(r)(6) claim that can void the collection effort.

Section 501(r)(6) - Extraordinary Collection Action Bar

The 501(r)(6) rule is one of the most under-used patient protections. It requires tax-exempt hospitals to:

Wait at least 120 days from first billing before any extraordinary collection action (ECA).

Provide a plain-language summary of the FAP with each bill during the 120-day window.

Accept FAP applications for at least 240 days from first billing.

Extraordinary collection actions include:

Credit reporting the debt

Filing a lawsuit

Placing a lien on property

Garnishing wages

Seizing bank accounts

If your Oklahoma hospital took any ECA without FAP screening, file a complaint with the IRS and demand retraction of the collection action.

CFPB 2025 Federal Medical-Debt Rule

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 2025 rule removes most medical debt from consumer credit reports nationwide, including in Oklahoma. The rule specifically:

Prohibits creditors from using medical information in most credit decisions.

Removes medical-debt collection tradelines under $500 after 1 year.

Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing medical-debt information for non-medical credit decisions.

The rule is separate from state-law bans and works in parallel. Where Oklahoma has its own state-law ban, the stricter rule controls.

Pre-Litigation Notice in Oklahoma

Oklahoma Consumer Protection Act

Many states now require hospitals to send a pre-suit notice offering a payment plan, FAP application, or charity-care screening before filing a collection lawsuit. In Oklahoma, the key pre-suit protections are captured in the rule above.

If the Oklahoma hospital skipped the notice or payment-plan offer, you may have:

A state-law claim to dismiss the lawsuit

An FDCPA claim against the collector (for attempting to collect on a defective claim)

A state unfair-trade-practices claim against the hospital

Medical Bill vs Medical Debt - Why the Distinction Matters in Oklahoma

This site focuses on medical bills: pre-discharge invoices from hospitals, providers, and specialists before they are sold to debt buyers. Bills have:

A direct provider relationship (you can negotiate, apply for FAP, set up payment plans)

Stronger legal protections (501(r), state HFA laws, pre-suit notice)

Higher negotiation leverage (providers will often accept 30-50% of billed)

Medical debt (covered at medicaldebtbankruptcy.com) is what the bill becomes after it is sold, charged off, or litigated:

Held by debt buyers, not providers

Subject to FDCPA and debt-validation rules

Often bought for 2-5 cents on the dollar, so settlements possible at steep discount

Strategy on the bill stage (this site) focuses on preventing the debt. Strategy on the debt stage focuses on resolving it.

Oklahoma Federal Bankruptcy Data

When hospital medical bills exceed income-based payment plans, bankruptcy discharges the debt and protects future wages and accounts. These FJC numbers show how Oklahoma debtors use the bankruptcy remedy for unpayable medical bills.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 112 consumer bankruptcy cases from Oklahoma's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 711099.1%0.9%

Chapter 132n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Bankruptcy as a Medical-Bill Discharge Tool in Oklahoma

When medical bills exceed your ability to pay through FAP, payment plans, and negotiation, bankruptcy discharges them. Medical debt is typically a general unsecured claim with no special treatment - it discharges in Chapter 7 within 90 days and is paid pro rata (often at cents on the dollar) through a Chapter 13 plan.

Key bankruptcy tools for Oklahoma medical debtors:

Chapter 7 discharge within 90-120 days

11 U.S.C. 362 automatic stay halts collection, garnishment, and lawsuit within 24 hours

11 U.S.C. 522(f) judicial lien avoidance against medical judgments impairing exemptions

Chapter 13 hardship discharge if medical condition prevents plan completion

Check 1328(f) refiling screener and the Oklahoma means test.

State medical-debt CR banSTATE BAN

Primary citationSDCL 54-3

Hospital financial-assistance (FAP)IRC 501(r)(4)

Price-transparency mandateNo state beyond federal

Pre-litigation rulesSD Deceptive Trade Practices Act

This page is about medical bills - the pre-discharge hospital invoices that have not yet been sold, charged off, or litigated. For post-collection medical debt that has already cycled through lawsuits and credit reporting, see the companion site medicaldebtbankruptcy.com.

Hospital Financial-Assistance Policy (FAP) Requirement in South Dakota

IRC 501(r)(4)

IRC 501(r)(4) is the federal baseline for non-profit hospitals: to maintain tax-exempt status, the hospital must adopt a written Financial Assistance Policy, widely publicize it, and offer discounted or free care to eligible patients. The 2014 IRS final rule also requires:

501(r)(5) limitation on charges: FAP-eligible patients cannot be charged more than the "amount generally billed" (AGB) to insured patients.

501(r)(6) billing and collection: No extraordinary collection actions until the hospital has made reasonable efforts to determine FAP eligibility.

If your South Dakota hospital skipped FAP screening before sending your bill to collections, you have a Section 501(r)(6) claim that can void the collection effort.

Section 501(r)(6) - Extraordinary Collection Action Bar

The 501(r)(6) rule is one of the most under-used patient protections. It requires tax-exempt hospitals to:

Wait at least 120 days from first billing before any extraordinary collection action (ECA).

Provide a plain-language summary of the FAP with each bill during the 120-day window.

Accept FAP applications for at least 240 days from first billing.

Extraordinary collection actions include:

Credit reporting the debt

Filing a lawsuit

Placing a lien on property

Garnishing wages

Seizing bank accounts

If your South Dakota hospital took any ECA without FAP screening, file a complaint with the IRS and demand retraction of the collection action.

CFPB 2025 Federal Medical-Debt Rule

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 2025 rule removes most medical debt from consumer credit reports nationwide, including in South Dakota. The rule specifically:

Prohibits creditors from using medical information in most credit decisions.

Removes medical-debt collection tradelines under $500 after 1 year.

Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing medical-debt information for non-medical credit decisions.

The rule is separate from state-law bans and works in parallel. Where South Dakota has its own state-law ban, the stricter rule controls.

Pre-Litigation Notice in South Dakota

SD Deceptive Trade Practices Act

Many states now require hospitals to send a pre-suit notice offering a payment plan, FAP application, or charity-care screening before filing a collection lawsuit. In South Dakota, the key pre-suit protections are captured in the rule above.

If the South Dakota hospital skipped the notice or payment-plan offer, you may have:

A state-law claim to dismiss the lawsuit

An FDCPA claim against the collector (for attempting to collect on a defective claim)

A state unfair-trade-practices claim against the hospital

Medical Bill vs Medical Debt - Why the Distinction Matters in South Dakota

This site focuses on medical bills: pre-discharge invoices from hospitals, providers, and specialists before they are sold to debt buyers. Bills have:

A direct provider relationship (you can negotiate, apply for FAP, set up payment plans)

Stronger legal protections (501(r), state HFA laws, pre-suit notice)

Higher negotiation leverage (providers will often accept 30-50% of billed)

Medical debt (covered at medicaldebtbankruptcy.com) is what the bill becomes after it is sold, charged off, or litigated:

Held by debt buyers, not providers

Subject to FDCPA and debt-validation rules

Often bought for 2-5 cents on the dollar, so settlements possible at steep discount

Strategy on the bill stage (this site) focuses on preventing the debt. Strategy on the debt stage focuses on resolving it.

Bankruptcy as a Medical-Bill Discharge Tool in South Dakota

When medical bills exceed your ability to pay through FAP, payment plans, and negotiation, bankruptcy discharges them. Medical debt is typically a general unsecured claim with no special treatment - it discharges in Chapter 7 within 90 days and is paid pro rata (often at cents on the dollar) through a Chapter 13 plan.

Key bankruptcy tools for South Dakota medical debtors:

Chapter 7 discharge within 90-120 days

11 U.S.C. 362 automatic stay halts collection, garnishment, and lawsuit within 24 hours

11 U.S.C. 522(f) judicial lien avoidance against medical judgments impairing exemptions

Chapter 13 hardship discharge if medical condition prevents plan completion

Check 1328(f) refiling screener and the South Dakota means test.

Medical debt exemptions

Hospital lien avoidance

Virginia Medical Bill Bankruptcy and Credit Reporting [2026]

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Virginia residents.

Virginia Medical Bill and Credit Reporting Protection

Virginia relies on the federal CFPB 2025 medical-debt rule and the Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. 1681). The CFPB rule removes most medical debt from credit reports nationwide starting 2025; Virginia has not yet enacted a state-specific supplement.

RuleVirginia Standard

State medical-debt CR banFEDERAL ONLY

Primary citationVa. Code 6.2-2500

Hospital financial-assistance (FAP)IRC 501(r)(4); VA Hospital Community Benefit

Price-transparency mandateVA Hospital Price Transparency

Pre-litigation rulesVirginia Consumer Protection Act

This page is about medical bills - the pre-discharge hospital invoices that have not yet been sold, charged off, or litigated. For post-collection medical debt that has already cycled through lawsuits and credit reporting, see the companion site medicaldebtbankruptcy.com.

Hospital Financial-Assistance Policy (FAP) Requirement in Virginia

IRC 501(r)(4); VA Hospital Community Benefit

IRC 501(r)(4) is the federal baseline for non-profit hospitals: to maintain tax-exempt status, the hospital must adopt a written Financial Assistance Policy, widely publicize it, and offer discounted or free care to eligible patients. The 2014 IRS final rule also requires:

501(r)(5) limitation on charges: FAP-eligible patients cannot be charged more than the "amount generally billed" (AGB) to insured patients.

501(r)(6) billing and collection: No extraordinary collection actions until the hospital has made reasonable efforts to determine FAP eligibility.

If your Virginia hospital skipped FAP screening before sending your bill to collections, you have a Section 501(r)(6) claim that can void the collection effort.

Section 501(r)(6) - Extraordinary Collection Action Bar

The 501(r)(6) rule is one of the most under-used patient protections. It requires tax-exempt hospitals to:

Wait at least 120 days from first billing before any extraordinary collection action (ECA).

Provide a plain-language summary of the FAP with each bill during the 120-day window.

Accept FAP applications for at least 240 days from first billing.

Extraordinary collection actions include:

Credit reporting the debt

Filing a lawsuit

Placing a lien on property

Garnishing wages

Seizing bank accounts

If your Virginia hospital took any ECA without FAP screening, file a complaint with the IRS and demand retraction of the collection action.

CFPB 2025 Federal Medical-Debt Rule

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 2025 rule removes most medical debt from consumer credit reports nationwide, including in Virginia. The rule specifically:

Prohibits creditors from using medical information in most credit decisions.

Removes medical-debt collection tradelines under $500 after 1 year.

Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing medical-debt information for non-medical credit decisions.

The rule is separate from state-law bans and works in parallel. Where Virginia has its own state-law ban, the stricter rule controls.

Pre-Litigation Notice in Virginia

Virginia Consumer Protection Act

Many states now require hospitals to send a pre-suit notice offering a payment plan, FAP application, or charity-care screening before filing a collection lawsuit. In Virginia, the key pre-suit protections are captured in the rule above.

If the Virginia hospital skipped the notice or payment-plan offer, you may have:

A state-law claim to dismiss the lawsuit

An FDCPA claim against the collector (for attempting to collect on a defective claim)

A state unfair-trade-practices claim against the hospital

Medical Bill vs Medical Debt - Why the Distinction Matters in Virginia

This site focuses on medical bills: pre-discharge invoices from hospitals, providers, and specialists before they are sold to debt buyers. Bills have:

A direct provider relationship (you can negotiate, apply for FAP, set up payment plans)

Stronger legal protections (501(r), state HFA laws, pre-suit notice)

Higher negotiation leverage (providers will often accept 30-50% of billed)

Medical debt (covered at medicaldebtbankruptcy.com) is what the bill becomes after it is sold, charged off, or litigated:

Held by debt buyers, not providers

Subject to FDCPA and debt-validation rules

Often bought for 2-5 cents on the dollar, so settlements possible at steep discount

Strategy on the bill stage (this site) focuses on preventing the debt. Strategy on the debt stage focuses on resolving it.

Virginia Federal Bankruptcy Data

When hospital medical bills exceed income-based payment plans, bankruptcy discharges the debt and protects future wages and accounts. These FJC numbers show how Virginia debtors use the bankruptcy remedy for unpayable medical bills.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,064 consumer bankruptcy cases from Virginia's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7514n/an/a

Chapter 1355071.2%28.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Bankruptcy as a Medical-Bill Discharge Tool in Virginia

When medical bills exceed your ability to pay through FAP, payment plans, and negotiation, bankruptcy discharges them. Medical debt is typically a general unsecured claim with no special treatment - it discharges in Chapter 7 within 90 days and is paid pro rata (often at cents on the dollar) through a Chapter 13 plan.

Key bankruptcy tools for Virginia medical debtors:

Chapter 7 discharge within 90-120 days

11 U.S.C. 362 automatic stay halts collection, garnishment, and lawsuit within 24 hours

11 U.S.C. 522(f) judicial lien avoidance against medical judgments impairing exemptions

Chapter 13 hardship discharge if medical condition prevents plan completion

Check 1328(f) refiling screener and the Virginia means test.
